subtype: Approach: puts a waiting rule on spending decisions [Revision]
passage:
Sangeeta: Your wishlist is open again. Wireless earbuds this time?
Bidisha: Not buying them tonight. Two-day rule, remember? Anything over a thousand rupees goes in my notes app and waits.
Sangeeta: Since when?
Bidisha: Since the third pair of shoes I never wore. Last week I listed a speaker, a jacket and a sketchbook set. Two days later I didn't even want the speaker.
Sangeeta: And the jacket?
Bidisha: Still want it. The zip on my old one snapped on Monday and waiting didn't fix that. So I'm ordering it now, and it feels calmer than before.
Sangeeta: So the rule isn't stopping you from buying things.
Bidisha: Only the things I wanted for one evening. 🙂

qa.q: Where does Bidisha keep the list of things that must wait?
qa.a: Bidisha keeps them in the notes app, since anything over a thousand rupees goes in my notes app and waits.

qa.q: What was Bidisha feeling when ordering the jacket?
qa.a: Bidisha felt calm and sure, because the want was still there after two days and the old zip really had snapped.

qa.q: What other approach could Bidisha add for an item that breaks and is needed right away?
qa.a: Bidisha could first ask whether the item is a real need today, because a broken zip cannot wait the way a speaker can.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta see the two-day rule after hearing about the jacket?
qa.a: Sangeeta may see it as a filter, not a ban, since Bidisha still bought the jacket that was truly needed.

grounding: A student's waiting rule on bigger purchases drops passing urges but keeps the real need.

subtype: Approach: uses quick action deliberately when the situation is urgent and stakes are small [Thinking]
passage:
Minakshi: Sorry, I'll be two minutes late to standup. Sorting out the corridor.
Mohit: What happened?
Minakshi: Somebody's coffee all over the floor by the printers. Grabbed the pantry mop straight away.
Mohit: Couldn't you just tell facilities?
Minakshi: Thought about it. Raise a ticket, wait, watch people skate past the puddle. The mop takes three minutes and nothing can go badly wrong here. This wasn't a moment for a plan.
Mohit: Fair. Someone was already tiptoeing round it 😅
Minakshi: Exactly. If it had been broken glass I'd have called someone in. Just a spill though 🙂
Mohit: Okay, standup starts when you're back.

qa.q: Where was the spill that Minakshi mopped up?
qa.a: It was on the floor by the printers in the corridor.

qa.q: What did Minakshi think about waiting for facilities?
qa.a: Minakshi thought raising a ticket would take longer than the job itself, and felt confident that mopping was simple and safe.

qa.q: What would be a wiser approach if the mess were broken glass?
qa.a: Calling someone in would be wiser, because the situation would no longer be small and simple, as Minakshi says.

qa.q: How does Mohit see Minakshi's choice to skip the ticket?
qa.a: Mohit accepts it as fair, and the colleague already tiptoeing round the puddle shows others were being bothered by it.

grounding: A colleague deliberately acts fast on an urgent, low-stakes spill instead of making a plan.

subtype: Approach: repeats the same method although it is not working [Pitfall]
passage:
Saturday. Tejas here. My drawer got stuck today and my maths set was inside. I pulled. Then I pulled harder. Then I put my foot on the wall and pulled with both hands. It went bang but it did not open. My fingers hurt a lot.
Mummy stood at the door with my bag and said we would be late for tuition. I pulled ten more times, maybe. Same thing. Nothing changed at all.
Now I am borrowing my sister's maths set, and it has a bent compass. I am still cross with the drawer. Tomorrow I will pull even harder.

qa.q: How did Tejas try to open the stuck drawer?
qa.a: Tejas pulled, then pulled harder, then put a foot on the wall and pulled with both hands.

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling at the end of the diary entry?
qa.a: Tejas felt cross with the drawer and still wanted to open it by pulling even harder.

qa.q: What different thing could Tejas try, and why?
qa.a: Tejas could lift the drawer a little or look inside to see what is stuck, since more pulling has not changed anything.

qa.q: How might Mummy see the drawer struggle?
qa.a: Mummy was waiting at the door with the bag, so may feel worried about being late and see the pulling as using up time.

grounding: A boy keeps pushing and pulling a jammed drawer harder without lifting it or checking what is stuck.

subtype: Approach: keeps studying the same way despite poor results [Pitfall]
passage:
Dear Chandrika,
Results came out. Chemistry, 41 out of 100, again. I don't get it. I sat with the notes for five hours the night before and read every page twice, highlighting in three colours.
Amma says maybe I should try some other way, but rereading is what I have done since class six and it feels like real studying. At night everything looked familiar, so I was sure I knew it. Then the paper asked me to explain things and my mind went blank.
The next exam is in three weeks. I think I'll start earlier and reread more.
Write back soon.
Ashwin

qa.q: How long did Ashwin sit with the notes the night before the paper?
qa.a: Ashwin sat with the notes for five hours and read every page twice.

qa.q: What does Ashwin feel about the way of studying used so far?
qa.a: Ashwin feels attached to rereading and trusts it, saying it feels like real studying even though the marks stayed low.

qa.q: What different approach could Ashwin try before the next exam, and why?
qa.a: Ashwin could close the notes and test by answering questions from memory, since the paper asked for explanations and rereading only made the pages look familiar.

qa.q: How might Amma feel about the plan to reread more?
qa.a: Amma already suggested some other way, so may feel worried that Ashwin will repeat what has not worked.

grounding: A student rereads notes for hours, scores poorly and does not try self-testing because rereading is the habit.

subtype: Approach: notices no progress and asks what could be different [Revision]
passage:
Hi, I'm Dev, and yes, the turning point was a physics test. I got 18 out of 50, and I had read that chapter three times. I sat there and asked myself, if this isn't working, what could be different?
Then I noticed something. When I read, everything felt easy. When I tried an actual question, I couldn't even start. So reading wasn't teaching me to remember.
That night I read for twenty minutes, closed the book and wrote what I could recall. The gaps were obvious. I did practice questions for the gaps.
Next test I got 34. Mrs Kulkarni asked what had changed, and I said, I stopped rereading and started recalling. She looked surprised, and pleased.

qa.q: How many marks did Dev get in the physics test?
qa.a: Dev got 18 out of 50.

qa.q: What did Dev feel about the low mark that made Dev ask what could be different?
qa.a: Dev felt puzzled and dissatisfied, since reading the chapter three times had not worked.

qa.q: What could Dev try next if recalling from memory stopped helping?
qa.a: Dev could ask Mrs Kulkarni which kinds of questions to practise, because a new signal of no progress would call for another change.

qa.q: How does Mrs Kulkarni see the change in Dev's marks?
qa.a: Mrs Kulkarni looked surprised and pleased when she asked what had changed and heard about the switch to recalling.

grounding: After a low mark a teenager asks what could change, tries practice questions and finds recalling beats rereading.

subtype: Approach: sticks with a plan out of pride even after the facts change [Pitfall]
passage:
So, you asked about the worst decision I made as event head. It was the date. I'm Ritika, and I'd announced the fest for the fourteenth on the notice board and in the group chat, with a poster and everything.
Five days before, the hall cancelled. My team said, move it a week. I said no. I'd told the whole college. They showed me the calendar, the exam schedule, everything, and I just kept saying, the fourteenth is the fourteenth.
So we ran it in the open courtyard, at noon, with a borrowed speaker. The heat sent half the audience away, and our guest was late. Danish, our treasurer, didn't speak to me for days.
Honestly? I wasn't protecting the fest. I was protecting my announcement.

qa.q: Where was the fest finally held?
qa.a: The fest was held in the open courtyard, at noon, with a borrowed speaker.

qa.q: What does Ritika feel when looking back on refusing to change the date?
qa.a: Ritika feels proud and a little ashamed, admitting the refusal protected the announcement, not the fest.

qa.q: What could Ritika have done when the hall cancelled?
qa.a: Ritika could have looked at the calendar with the team and moved the fest a week, since the venue fact had changed, and told everyone the new date.

qa.q: How did Danish see the way the date was handled?
qa.a: Danish, the treasurer, was upset enough to stay silent for days, so the choice cost the team goodwill as well as turnout.

grounding: A student leader refuses to move the event date after the venue cancels because of a public announcement.

subtype: Approach: keeps a firm goal but changes the method [Revision]
passage:
Himani: Any news on the Pune delivery?
Sahil: Bad news. The highway is shut past Nashik after the landslide. Trucks can't get through till next week.
Himani: The client's launch is on the 12th. That date stays.
Sahil: Then how do we get there?
Himani: Rail. Does the goods yard have a slot?
Sahil: Checking... yes, the 9th. We'd have to load at the station, and it costs more.
Himani: Book it. Tell the client the route changed, not the date.
Sahil: On it 👍
Himani: The truck was only ever a way to get there 🙂

qa.q: Which day is the client's launch?
qa.a: The client's launch is on the 12th.

qa.q: How does Himani seem to feel about the closed highway?
qa.a: Himani seems calm and determined, keeping the client's date of the 12th fixed and treating the truck as only one way to get there.

qa.q: What else could Himani try if the rail slot on the 9th fell through?
qa.a: Himani could ask about another route or split the load, since the goal is still the date and any working way to reach it will do.

qa.q: How does the change look to Sahil, who has to arrange it?
qa.a: Sahil has to load at the station and handle a higher cost, so may see it as more work, though it saves the date.

grounding: A manager keeps the delivery goal but changes the method from road to rail when the route is blocked.

subtype: Approach: persistence as a strength on a hard long task [Thinking]
passage:
Supervisor's note on Nikita's seedling experiment.
The fifth run failed today, like the four before it. Nikita did not repeat it. She changed one detail each time: soil moisture after the second run, the hour of measuring after the third, the lamp distance after the fourth.
I asked why she keeps going. She said the first two runs both leaned the same way, so the effect is probably real and each failure tells her which detail to fix. She writes down what she changed and why, every evening.
I have given her the second growth room for next week and asked nothing else of her. I'll read the log on Friday.

qa.q: What did Nikita change after the third run?
qa.a: Nikita changed the hour of measuring after the third run.

qa.q: How does Nikita seem to feel after five failed runs?
qa.a: Nikita seems patient and hopeful, believing the effect is probably real since the first two runs leaned the same way.

qa.q: What could Nikita try if the effect still did not show after many more changes?
qa.a: Nikita could ask a colleague to run the same setup independently, since another pair of hands would show whether the problem lies in the method or in the idea.

qa.q: How does the supervisor see Nikita's way of working?
qa.a: The supervisor sees careful, patient work, and shows it by giving Nikita the second growth room and planning to read the log on Friday.

grounding: A researcher keeps refining an experiment through failures because earlier results suggest the effect is real.

subtype: Approach: fears making the wrong choice and keeps gathering data [Thinking]
passage:
Monday. Madhuri has to pick an elective by Friday, art or computer basics. She asks her cousin, then a teacher, then reads two articles. Each says something different. She thinks, one more opinion and I'll know which is safe.
Thursday. Noor finds her with eleven tabs open. "What's the new one?" "A forum about which elective helps most later." "Later when?" "I don't know. That's the problem." She opens a twelfth. "There has to be a choice that can't go wrong."
Next Tuesday. The form went in a day late with computer basics ticked. Madhuri's shoulders are tight. "What if art was the right one?" Noor shrugs. "There wasn't a safe one, remember?"

qa.q: How many tabs did Madhuri have open on Thursday?
qa.a: Madhuri had eleven tabs open, and then opened a twelfth.

qa.q: What was Madhuri afraid of while asking more people and reading more?
qa.a: Madhuri feared choosing the wrong elective and hoped to find one that can't go wrong.

qa.q: What could Madhuri try instead of gathering more opinions?
qa.a: Madhuri could set a stopping point, such as one more conversation and then a choice, since no amount of information removes all risk.

qa.q: How does Noor see Madhuri's search?
qa.a: Noor sees that there was never a safe option to find, and gently reminds Madhuri of this after the form is in.

grounding: A teenager fears the wrong elective and keeps gathering data hoping for a risk-free choice.

subtype: Approach: compares options endlessly without deciding [Pitfall]
passage:
The reviews for the first laptop looked fine. Then Yara found a video about a second one, and a forum thread warning about a third. By the end of the first week there were twenty laptops in a spreadsheet, and every new page added a doubt.
"Does it get hot?" "Is the battery honest in the reviews?" Felix, who shared the flat, watched her scroll one evening. "It's been three weeks. Just pick one." "Then I'll read one more comparison." 
Her old laptop crashed during a group assignment, and Yara finished at the library, queuing for a free computer. The spreadsheet still had no winner.

qa.q: How many laptops did Yara have in the spreadsheet?
qa.a: Yara had twenty laptops in the spreadsheet.

qa.q: What was Yara feeling as each new review appeared?
qa.a: Yara felt doubt, since every new page added a worry instead of making the choice clearer.

qa.q: What different approach could Yara use to end the search?
qa.a: Yara could list the three things that matter most and pick the first laptop that meets them, since good enough would end the loop.

qa.q: How does Felix see the three weeks of reading?
qa.a: Felix has watched it for weeks and wants Yara to just pick one, seeing more reading as unlikely to help.

grounding: A student compares twenty laptops for weeks without deciding, and new information only adds doubt.
